svg.title: The Node.js Architecture Behind the Scenes
svg.desc: Auto-playing 56s step-by-step explainer of "The Node.js Architecture Behind the Scenes" (from img_5.png). Each step is highlighted in turn with what happens, why it matters, missing concepts added in lime, and a Node.js code example. Hover to pause.
svg.text: The Node.js Architecture Behind the Scenes
From your 100% JavaScript code down through Node, V8, libuv and the C/C++ libraries to the OS
Runs it on the call stack

g.text: The Node.js Architecture Behind the Scenes
What: Your JS calls Node's APIs. Node passes the work to V8 (to run JS) and libuv (to do
async I/O), which use small C/C++ libraries for HTTP, DNS, TLS and compression.
Why: Knowing the layers explains why Node is fast, what the thread pool is for, and where
Added: The C++ bindings layer that connects JS to C/C++, today's dependencies (llhttp
replaced http-parser), and which work really uses the thread pool.
V8 (runs JS) libuv (event loop + thread pool)
What: The only layer you write: plain JavaScript that calls Node APIs like fs.readFile or
Why: You get C++ speed for I/O without ever writing C++.
// you only ever write this layer
What: Node's own standard library is written in JavaScript (lib/fs.js, lib/http.js...).
Underneath, C++ "bindings" expose C/C++ functions to that JavaScript.
Added: The bindings layer is the missing piece on the slide: it is how one JS call ends up
as a system call in the OS.
the event loop runs it later
What: V8 turns your JavaScript into machine code and runs it. It also owns the memory heap
Why: Without V8 Node could not understand any JavaScript at all.
Added: You can tune and inspect V8 from Node: bigger heap with --max-old-space-size,
for (let i = 0; i < 1e7; i++) hot(i); // V8 JIT-optimises "hot"
What: libuv gives Node async I/O on every OS. It implements the event loop and a thread pool
Added: Network I/O does not use the thread pool: libuv asks the OS kernel (epoll on Linux,
kqueue on macOS, IOCP on Windows). Pool size: UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE.
What: Small specialised libraries do the low-level jobs: parse HTTP, resolve DNS, encrypt
Added: http-parser was replaced by llhttp (Node 12+). Newer ones: nghttp2 (HTTP/2), ICU
What: Your JS → Node core → bindings → V8 runs the JS, libuv does the async work → C/C++
libs → OS. Results come back as callbacks.
Added: C++ bindings, llhttp / nghttp2 / undici, libuv in C, and network I/O going through
the OS instead of the thread pool.

svg.text: V8 runs JS · libuv does async I/O
Thinking all async work uses the thread pool
→ network I/O goes to the OS kernel
Q: What do V8 and libuv each do?
A: V8 executes JS; libuv = loop + async I/O
